content: The following are professional descriptions of the studies and programs mentioned: 1. In 2007, a study by Tal et al. examined the use of buprenorphine-naloxone treatment for opioid-dependent inmates in Puerto Rico prior to their release. The findings were published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine, highlighting the potential benefits of this treatment approach in correctional settings. 2. Hedrich and Alves, in 2012, conducted a systematic review on the effectiveness of opioid maintenance treatment in prison environments. Their research, published in Addiction, demonstrated the positive impact of such treatments on reducing opioid use and associated risks among incarcerated individuals. 3. Sacks and McKendrick, in 2012, carried out a randomized clinical trial to evaluate therapeutic community treatment for female inmates. The study assessed outcomes at six and twelve months post-release, with results published in the Journal of Addictive Diseases, emphasizing the importance of structured therapeutic interventions for this population. 4. Springer and Chen, in 2010, investigated the outcomes of buprenorphine treatment for HIV-infected prisoners post-release. Their study, published in the Journal of Urban Health, showed improved HIV and substance abuse treatment outcomes, underscoring the role of medication-assisted therapy in this context. 5. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) released a 2013 report detailing the implementation of opioid substitution therapy (OST) in Tihar prisons, India. This scientific report highlighted the program's success in addressing opioid dependence among inmates. 6. Freudenberg and Ramaswamy, in 2010, evaluated the REAL MEN re-entry program, which aimed to reduce drug use, HIV risk, and recidivism among young men leaving jail. Published in the Journal of Adolescent Health, the study demonstrated the program's effectiveness in addressing these critical issues. 7. De la Fuente and Bravo, in 2012, analyzed the evolution of opioid substitution treatment and needle exchange programs in Spanish prisons from 1992 to 2009. Their findings, published in Revista Española de Sanidad Penitenciaria, highlighted the increasing coverage and impact of these harm reduction strategies. 8. Bachireddy and Bazazi, in 2011, explored attitudes toward opioid substitution therapy and pre-incarceration HIV transmission behaviors among HIV-infected prisoners in Malaysia. Their study, published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence, provided insights into secondary prevention strategies for this population. 9. Favrod-Coune and Baroundi, in 2013, presented a case study on opioid substitution treatment in pretrial detention in Geneva, Switzerland. Published in the Swiss Medical Weekly, the study emphasized the importance of early intervention for opioid-dependent detainees. 10. Eshrati and Asl, in 2008, examined the initial support for harm reduction education to prevent HIV transmission among Iranian prisoners. Their findings, published in the Harm Reduction Journal, highlighted the benefits of educational interventions in correctional settings. 11. Derlega and Winstead, in 2008, investigated AIDS-related stigma among inmates and staff in a U.S. state prison. Published in the Journal of STD and AIDS, the study shed light on the challenges of addressing stigma in correctional environments. 12. Fields and Gonzalez, in 2008, emphasized the importance of learning from incarcerated women to improve health interventions. Their work highlighted the unique needs and experiences of this population. 13. Sifunda and Reddy, in 2008, evaluated the effectiveness of a peer-led HIV/AIDS and STI health education intervention for prison inmates. Published in Health Education and Behavior, the study demonstrated the value of peer-led approaches in improving health outcomes. 14. Ko and Hsu, in 2009, conducted a pilot study on HIV education's impact on substance use readiness, AIDS knowledge, and self-efficacy among male drug-dependent inmates. Their findings, published in Substance Use and Misuse, highlighted the potential of targeted educational programs. 15. Grinstead and Eldridge, in 2008, developed an HIV, STD, and hepatitis prevention program for young men leaving prison, known as Project START. Published in the Journal of Correctional Health Care, the program demonstrated success in reducing risk behaviors. 16. Fluhmann and Wassmer, in 2012, discussed the structured exchange of information on infectious diseases for prisoners. Published in the Journal of Correctional Health Care, the study emphasized the importance of effective communication in managing infectious diseases in correctional settings. 17. Goldberg and Millson, in 2009, conducted a randomized controlled trial on an HIV risk reduction intervention for incarcerated youth. Published in the Journal of Adolescent Health, the study highlighted the intervention's effectiveness in reducing risky behaviors. 18. Gurdin and Niego, in 2008, described the Rikers Health Advocacy Program (RHAP), an STI/HIV/AIDS prevention program for young men. This program was featured in a model programs guide for adolescent sexual health. 19. Hurd and Valerio, in 2010, adapted an HIV prevention intervention for high-risk incarcerated adolescents. Published in Health Education and Behavior, the study demonstrated the importance of tailoring interventions to meet the needs of this population. 20. Martin and O’Connell, in 2008, integrated an HIV/HCV brief intervention into prisoner re-entry programs. Published in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, the study highlighted the benefits of addressing co-infections during re-entry. 21. La Vigne and Debus-Sherrill, in 2011, explored strategies to prevent violence and sexual assault in jails using a situational crime prevention approach. Their findings were published in a Justice Policy Center brief. 22. Yap and Richters, in 2011, documented the decline in sexual assaults in men’s prisons in New South Wales, attributing the success to a systems approach. Published in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence, the study emphasized the importance of systemic interventions. 23. Ravi and Blankenship, in 2007, examined women’s health issues in correctional settings, focusing on the unique challenges faced by incarcerated women. Their findings were published in Women’s Health Issues. 24. Kerbs and Jolley, in 2007, investigated inmate-on-inmate victimization among older male prisoners. Published in Crime and Delinquency, the study highlighted the vulnerabilities of this population. 25. Kavasery and Maru, in 2009, conducted a prospective controlled trial on routine opt-out HIV testing in a female jail setting. Published in PLoS One, the study demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of routine testing. 26. Duffus and Youmans, in 2009, identified missed opportunities for early HIV diagnosis in correctional facilities. Published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs, the study emphasized the need for improved testing strategies. 27. Jafa and McElroy, in 2009, provided empirical support for jail-based HIV testing. Published in PLoS One, the study highlighted the importance of early identification of HIV in correctional settings. 28. Motshabi and Pengpid, in 2011, examined the utilization and attitudes toward HIV counseling and testing among male inmates in a South African prison. Published in the Journal of Social Aspects of HIV/AIDS, the study emphasized the need for accessible testing services. 29. De Voux and Spaulding, in 2012, provided evidence for the effectiveness of jail-based HIV testing. Published in PLoS One, the study highlighted the benefits of early identification and linkage to care. 30. Beckwith and Liu, in 2010, evaluated HIV risk behaviors before and after counseling and testing in jail. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study demonstrated the impact of counseling on reducing risky behaviors. 31. MacGowan and Margolis, in 2009, assessed the feasibility of voluntary rapid HIV testing in jails. Published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases, the study highlighted the acceptability of rapid testing. 32. Beckwith and Bazerman, in 2011, evaluated a routine opt-out rapid HIV testing program in Rhode Island. Published in AIDS Education and Prevention, the study demonstrated the program’s success in increasing testing rates. 33. Tartaro and Levy, in 2012, evaluated an HIV testing program in a jail setting, providing recommendations for improvement. Published in The Prison Journal, the study emphasized the importance of routine testing. 34. Andrinopoulos and Kerrigan, in 2010, established an HIV/STD program for incarcerated men in Jamaica. Published in the International Journal of STD and AIDS, the study highlighted the program’s success in addressing infection prevalence. 35. Arp, in 2009, discussed the intersection of race, incarceration, and HIV/AIDS in Louisiana, advocating for mandatory testing to address risky sexual behaviors. Published in Race, Class, and Gender, the study emphasized the need for targeted interventions. 36. Kavasery and Maru, in 2009, conducted a prospective controlled trial on routine opt-out HIV testing in a men’s jail. Published in PLoS One, the study demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of routine testing. 37. Strick and MacGowan, in 2011, reported on HIV screening during prison intake medical evaluations in Washington. Published in MMWR, the study highlighted the importance of early screening. 38. Javanbakht and Murphy, in 2007, examined the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections and HIV among incarcerated men who have sex with men. Published in Sexually Transmitted Infections, the study emphasized the need for targeted prevention efforts. 39. Tuli and Kerndt, in 2009, conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of preventing sexually transmitted infections among incarcerated men who have sex with men. Published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases, the study highlighted the economic benefits of prevention programs. 40. Roberson and White, in 2009, identified factors influencing adherence to antiretroviral therapy among HIV-infected female inmates. Published in the Journal of the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care, the study emphasized the importance of addressing barriers to adherence. 41. Small and Wood, in 2009, explored the impact of incarceration on adherence to HIV treatment among injection drug users. Published in AIDS Care, the study highlighted the challenges faced by this population. 42. Shalihu and Pretorius, in 2014, described barriers to antiretroviral therapy adherence among Namibian prisoners. Published in AIDS Care, the study emphasized the need for targeted interventions. 43. Catz and Thibodeau, in 2011, identified the prevention needs of HIV-positive individuals awaiting release from prison. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study highlighted the importance of pre-release planning. 44. Fontana and Beckerman, in 2007, examined the primary care needs of recently released individuals with HIV/AIDS. Published in the Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, the study emphasized the importance of continuity of care. 45. Wohl and Scheyett, in 2011, compared intensive case management with comprehensive pre-release discharge planning for linking HIV-infected prisoners to care. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study found no significant difference in effectiveness. 46. Nunn and Cornwall, in 2010, assessed the COMPASS program, which linked HIV-positive jail inmates to treatment and social services post-release. Published in the Journal of Urban Health, the study highlighted the program’s success. 47. Zaller and Holmes, in 2008, evaluated Project Bridge, which provided linkage to treatment and supportive services for HIV-positive ex-offenders. Published in the Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, the study emphasized the importance of post-release support. 48. Seal and Margolis, in 2008, examined substance use and sexual behavior during incarceration among young men. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study highlighted the prevalence and correlates of risky behaviors. 49. Milloy and Kerr, in 2013, found that incarceration was associated with syringe lending among active injection drug users with detectable HIV-1 RNA. Published in BMC Infectious Diseases, the study emphasized the need for harm reduction programs. 50. Moller and Van Den Bergh, in 2008, studied the impact of health promotion on drug use in Kyrgyzstan prisons. Published in the International Journal of Prisoner Health, the study highlighted the benefits of health promotion initiatives. 51. Roshanfekr and Farnia, in 2013, evaluated the effectiveness of harm reduction programs in seven Iranian prisons. Published in the Iranian Journal of Public Health, the study demonstrated the success of these programs. 52. Ferrer-Castro and Crespo-Leiro, in 2012, reviewed a ten-year needle exchange program in a Spanish prison. Published in Revista Española de Sanidad Penitenciaria, the study highlighted the program’s long-term impact.
